claim: Sensitive periods are epochs during the lifespan within which effects of experience on the brain are particularly strong.
source: Sensitive periods are epochs during the lifespan within which effects of experience on the brain are particularly strong (Knudsen, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knudsen, 2004

claim: Structural remodelling strongly links to the timing of sensitive periods.
source: Non-human animal work has established that structural remodelling (Bourgeois, 1997) and the development of local inhibitory neural circuits strongly link to the timing of sensitive periods (Gianfranceschi et al., 2003; Hensch et al., 1998; Hensch and Bilimoria, 2012; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Takesian and Hensch, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to non-human animal work

claim: The development of local inhibitory neural circuits strongly links to the timing of sensitive periods.
source: Non-human animal work has established that structural remodelling (Bourgeois, 1997) and the development of local inhibitory neural circuits strongly link to the timing of sensitive periods (Gianfranceschi et al., 2003; Hensch et al., 1998; Hensch and Bilimoria, 2012; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Takesian and Hensch, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to non-human animal work

claim: Early visual experience fine-tunes local inhibitory circuits.
source: Early visual experience has been shown to fine-tune local inhibitory circuits (Benevento et al., 1992; Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004; Gandhi et al., 2008; Toyoizumi et al., 2013), which dynamically control feedforward excitation (Tao and Poo, 2005; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Local inhibitory circuits dynamically control feedforward excitation.
source: Early visual experience has been shown to fine-tune local inhibitory circuits (Benevento et al., 1992; Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004; Gandhi et al., 2008; Toyoizumi et al., 2013), which dynamically control feedforward excitation (Tao and Poo, 2005; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tao and Poo, 2005; Wu et al., 2022

claim: The end of the sensitive period coincides with the maturation of inhibitory neural circuits.
source: The end of the sensitive period has been proposed to coincide with the maturation of inhibitory neural circuits (Hensch, 2005a; Wong-Riley, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hensch, 2005a; Wong-Riley, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018

claim: Neural circuit stability following sensitive periods is maintained via a balance between excitatory and inhibitory transmission across multiple spatiotemporal scales.
source: Within this framework, neural circuit stability following sensitive periods is maintained via a balance between excitatory and inhibitory transmission across multiple spatiotemporal scales (Froemke, 2015; Haider et al., 2006; Maffei et al., 2004; Takesian and Hensch, 2013; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) ratio has been studied at different organizational levels, including the synaptic and neuronal levels, as well as for neural circuits.
source: Such an excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) ratio has been studied at different organizational levels, including the synaptic and neuronal levels, as well as for neural circuits (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Wu et al., 2022

claim: Studies of the mouse visual cortex demonstrated a disrupted tuning of local inhibitory circuits as a consequence of lacking visual experience at birth.
source: In particular, studies of the mouse visual cortex demonstrated a disrupted tuning of local inhibitory circuits as a consequence of lacking visual experience at birth (Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Levelt and Hübener, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Levelt and Hübener, 2012

claim: Dark-reared mice have increased spontaneous neural firing in adulthood.
source: In addition, dark-reared mice have been shown to have increased spontaneous neural firing in adulthood (Benevento et al., 1992) and a reduced magnitude of inhibition, particularly in layers II/III of the visual cortex (Morales et al., 2002), suggesting an overall higher level of excitation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Benevento et al., 1992

claim: Dark-reared mice have a reduced magnitude of inhibition, particularly in layers II/III of the visual cortex.
source: In addition, dark-reared mice have been shown to have increased spontaneous neural firing in adulthood (Benevento et al., 1992) and a reduced magnitude of inhibition, particularly in layers II/III of the visual cortex (Morales et al., 2002), suggesting an overall higher level of excitation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Morales et al., 2002

claim: Dark-reared mice have an overall higher level of excitation.
source: In addition, dark-reared mice have been shown to have increased spontaneous neural firing in adulthood (Benevento et al., 1992) and a reduced magnitude of inhibition, particularly in layers II/III of the visual cortex (Morales et al., 2002), suggesting an overall higher level of excitation.
evidence: Inferred from increased spontaneous firing and reduced inhibition in dark-reared mice

claim: Visual experience during the first weeks and months of life is crucial for the development of visual neural circuits.
source: Human neuroimaging studies have similarly demonstrated that visual experience during the first weeks and months of life is crucial for the development of visual neural circuits (Baroncelli et al., 2011; Lewis and Maurer, 2005; Maurer and Hensch, 2012; Röder et al., 2021; Röder et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to human neuroimaging studies

claim: Human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts treated later than a few weeks from birth suffer from a permanent reduction of visual acuity.
source: If human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts are treated later than a few weeks from birth, they suffer from a permanent reduction of visual acuity (Birch et al., 1998; Khanna et al., 2013), stereovision (Birch et al., 1993; Tytla et al., 1993), and impairments in higher level visual functions such as face perception (Le Grand et al., 2001; Putzar et al., 2010; Röder et al., 2013), coherent motion detection (Bottari et al., 2018; Hadad et al., 2012; Maurer and Lewis, 2018), visual temporal processing (Badde et al., 2020), and visual feature binding (McKyton et al., 2015; Putzar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birch et al., 1998; Khanna et al., 2013

claim: Human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts treated later than a few weeks from birth suffer from impairments in stereovision.
source: If human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts are treated later than a few weeks from birth, they suffer from a permanent reduction of visual acuity (Birch et al., 1998; Khanna et al., 2013), stereovision (Birch et al., 1993; Tytla et al., 1993), and impairments in higher level visual functions such as face perception (Le Grand et al., 2001; Putzar et al., 2010; Röder et al., 2013), coherent motion detection (Bottari et al., 2018; Hadad et al., 2012; Maurer and Lewis, 2018), visual temporal processing (Badde et al., 2020), and visual feature binding (McKyton et al., 2015; Putzar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birch et al., 1993; Tytla et al., 1993

evidence: Supported by citations to Le Grand et al., 2001; Putzar et al., 2010; Röder et al., 2013

evidence: Supported by citations to Bottari et al., 2018; Hadad et al., 2012; Maurer and Lewis, 2018

claim: Human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts treated later than a few weeks from birth suffer from impairments in visual temporal processing.
source: If human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts are treated later than a few weeks from birth, they suffer from a permanent reduction of visual acuity (Birch et al., 1998; Khanna et al., 2013), stereovision (Birch et al., 1993; Tytla et al., 1993), and impairments in higher level visual functions such as face perception (Le Grand et al., 2001; Putzar et al., 2010; Röder et al., 2013), coherent motion detection (Bottari et al., 2018; Hadad et al., 2012; Maurer and Lewis, 2018), visual temporal processing (Badde et al., 2020), and visual feature binding (McKyton et al., 2015; Putzar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Badde et al., 2020

claim: Human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts treated later than a few weeks from birth suffer from impairments in visual feature binding.
source: If human infants born with dense bilateral cataracts are treated later than a few weeks from birth, they suffer from a permanent reduction of visual acuity (Birch et al., 1998; Khanna et al., 2013), stereovision (Birch et al., 1993; Tytla et al., 1993), and impairments in higher level visual functions such as face perception (Le Grand et al., 2001; Putzar et al., 2010; Röder et al., 2013), coherent motion detection (Bottari et al., 2018; Hadad et al., 2012; Maurer and Lewis, 2018), visual temporal processing (Badde et al., 2020), and visual feature binding (McKyton et al., 2015; Putzar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKyton et al., 2015; Putzar et al., 2007

claim: Visual deficits in congenital cataract-reversal individuals have been attributed to altered neural development due to the absence of early visual experience.
source: These visual deficits in congenital cataract-reversal individuals have been attributed to altered neural development due to the absence of early visual experience, as individuals who suffered from developmental cataracts do not typically display a comparable severity of visual impairments (Lewis and Maurer, 2009; Sourav et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis and Maurer, 2009; Sourav et al., 2020

claim: Individuals who suffered from developmental cataracts do not typically display a comparable severity of visual impairments as congenital cataract-reversal individuals.
source: These visual deficits in congenital cataract-reversal individuals have been attributed to altered neural development due to the absence of early visual experience, as individuals who suffered from developmental cataracts do not typically display a comparable severity of visual impairments (Lewis and Maurer, 2009; Sourav et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis and Maurer, 2009; Sourav et al., 2020

claim: Correlations between structural changes and behavioral outcomes in congenital cataract-reversal individuals have been reported.
source: While the extant literature has reported correlations between structural changes and behavioral outcomes in congenital cataract-reversal individuals (Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023; Pedersini et al., 2023), functional brain imaging (Heitmann et al., 2023; Rączy et al., 2022) and electrophysiological research (Bottari et al., 2016; Ossandón et al., 2023; Pant et al., 2023; Pitchaimuthu et al., 2021) have started to unravel the neural mechanisms which rely on visual experience during early brain development.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023; Pedersini et al., 2023

claim: Functional brain imaging and electrophysiological research have started to unravel the neural mechanisms which rely on visual experience during early brain development.
source: While the extant literature has reported correlations between structural changes and behavioral outcomes in congenital cataract-reversal individuals (Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023; Pedersini et al., 2023), functional brain imaging (Heitmann et al., 2023; Rączy et al., 2022) and electrophysiological research (Bottari et al., 2016; Ossandón et al., 2023; Pant et al., 2023; Pitchaimuthu et al., 2021) have started to unravel the neural mechanisms which rely on visual experience during early brain development.
evidence: Supported by citations to functional brain imaging and electrophysiological research

claim: The amplitude of low frequency (<1 Hz; blood oxygen level-dependent) fluctuations (ALFF) in the visual cortex was increased in congenital cataract-reversal individuals compared to normally sighted controls when they were scanned with their eyes open.
source: Resting-state activity measured via fMRI suggested increased excitation in the visual cortex of congenital cataract-reversal individuals (Rączy et al., 2022): The amplitude of low frequency (<1 Hz; blood oxygen level-dependent) fluctuations (ALFF) in the visual cortex was increased in congenital cataract-reversal individuals compared to normally sighted controls when they were scanned with their eyes open.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rączy et al., 2022

claim: Similar changes in ALFF were observed in permanently congenitally blind humans.
source: Since similar changes were observed in permanently congenitally blind humans, the authors speculated that congenital visual deprivation resulted in an increased E/I ratio of neural circuits due to impaired neural tuning, which was not reinstated after sight restoration (Rączy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rączy et al., 2022

claim: Congenital visual deprivation resulted in an increased E/I ratio of neural circuits due to impaired neural tuning, which was not reinstated after sight restoration.
source: Since similar changes were observed in permanently congenitally blind humans, the authors speculated that congenital visual deprivation resulted in an increased E/I ratio of neural circuits due to impaired neural tuning, which was not reinstated after sight restoration (Rączy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation by authors cited in Rączy et al., 2022

claim: Resting-state EEG studies measured periodic (alpha oscillations) and aperiodic activity in congenital cataract-reversal individuals.
source: Other studies measured resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) activity and analyzed periodic (alpha oscillations) (Bottari et al., 2016; Ossandón et al., 2023; Pant et al., 2023) as well as aperiodic activity (Ossandón et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bottari et al., 2016; Ossandón et al., 2023; Pant et al., 2023

claim: Both periodic and aperiodic EEG measures pointed towards a higher E/I ratio of visual cortex in congenital cataract-reversal individuals.
source: Both measures pointed towards an higher E/I ratio of visual cortex in congenital cataract-reversal individuals (Ossandón et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ossandón et al., 2023

claim: The slope of the aperiodic component of the EEG power spectral density function is interpreted as an indirect indication of the relative level of excitation; the flatter the slope, the higher the assumed E/I ratio.
source: In recent research, authors have interpreted the slope of the aperiodic component of the EEG power spectral density function as an indirect indication of the relative level of excitation; the flatter the slope, the higher the assumed E/I ratio (Gao et al., 2017; Lombardi et al., 2017; McSweeney et al., 2023; Medel et al., 2020; Molina et al., 2020; Muthukumaraswamy and Liley, 2018; Nanda et al., 2023; Schaworonkow and Voytek, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Prospective studies in children have reported a flattening of the aperiodic slope with age, which was interpreted as increasing levels of excitation with age.
source: In fact, prospective studies in children have recently reported a flattening of this slope with age, which was interpreted as increasing levels of excitation with age (Favaro et al., 2023; Hill et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Favaro et al., 2023; Hill et al., 2022

claim: Ossandón et al., 2023 observed a flatter slope of the aperiodic power spectrum in the high-frequency range (20–40 Hz) but a steeper slope of the low-frequency range (1–19 Hz) in congenital cataract-reversal individuals and permanently congenitally blind humans.
source: Ossandón et al., 2023 observed a flatter slope of the aperiodic power spectrum in the high-frequency range (20–40 Hz) but a steeper slope of the low-frequency range (1–19 Hz). This pattern was found in both congenital cataract-reversal individuals, as well as in permanently congenitally blind humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ossandón et al., 2023

claim: The low-frequency range has often been associated with inhibition.
source: The low-frequency range has often been associated with inhibition (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Lozano-Soldevilla, 2018; Lozano-Soldevilla et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Lozano-Soldevilla, 2018; Lozano-Soldevilla et al., 2014

claim: Glutamate/Glutamine concentration was significantly increased in the 'visual' cortex of anophthalmic (n=5) compared to normally sighted individuals, suggesting increased excitability.
source: Glutamate/Glutamine concentration was significantly increased in the 'visual' cortex of anophthalmic (n=5) compared to normally sighted individuals, suggesting increased excitability (Coullon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coullon et al., 2015

claim: Preliminary evidence in congenitally permanently blind individuals (n=9) suggested a decreased GABA concentration in the visual cortex compared to normally sighted individuals.
source: Preliminary evidence in congenitally permanently blind individuals (n=9) suggested a decreased GABA concentration in the visual cortex compared to normally sighted individuals (Weaver et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weaver et al., 2013

claim: MRS studies corroborated the hypothesis that a lack of visual input at birth enhances relative excitation in visual cortex compared to typical brain development.
source: Thus, these MRS studies corroborated the hypothesis that a lack of visual input at birth enhances relative excitation in visual cortex compared to typical brain development.
evidence: Inferred from MRS studies showing increased Glx and decreased GABA in blind individuals

claim: The ratio of Glx/GABA+ concentration was used as a proxy for the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurotransmission.
source: The ratio of Glx/GABA+ concentration was used as a proxy for the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurotransmission (Gao et al., 2024; Grent-'t-Jong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2015; Narayan et al., 2022; Steel et al., 2020; Takei et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Both neurotransmitter levels and EEG aperiodic activity systematically vary between eyes open and eyes closed conditions.
source: Participants were tested with their eyes open, eyes closed (MRS and EEG), and while viewing visual stimuli (EEG) which changed in luminance (Pant et al., 2023), since both neurotransmitter levels (Kurcyus et al., 2018) and EEG aperiodic activity (Ossandón et al., 2023) systematically varies between these conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kurcyus et al., 2018 and Ossandón et al., 2023

claim: The aperiodic intercept has been linked to broad band neuronal firing.
source: Since the aperiodic intercept has been linked to broad band neuronal firing (Manning et al., 2009; Musall et al., 2014; Winawer et al., 2013) and based on prior findings suggesting higher excitation in congenital cataract-reversal individuals (Ossandón et al., 2023; Rączy et al., 2022), we predicted a higher intercept as well as an altered slope of the EEG aperiodic component in this group.
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning et al., 2009; Musall et al., 2014; Winawer et al., 2013

claim: The present results provide initial evidence for experience-dependent development of the E/I ratio in the human visual cortex, with consequences for behavior.

claim: The lower Glx/GABA+ ratio and steeper slope of the aperiodic EEG activity (1–20 Hz) at occipital electrodes suggest a lower rather than higher E/I ratio in the visual cortex of CC individuals.

claim: The results imply a change in neurotransmitter concentrations as a consequence of restoring vision following congenital blindness.
source: Here, we speculate that our results imply a change in neurotransmitter concentrations as a consequence of restoring vision following congenital blindness.

claim: Due to limited structural plasticity after a phase of congenital blindness, the neural circuits of CC individuals, which had adapted to blindness after birth, likely employ physiological plasticity mechanisms in order to re-adapt to the newly available visual excitation following sight restoration later in life.
source: Further, we hypothesize that due to limited structural plasticity after a phase of congenital blindness, the neural circuits of CC individuals, which had adapted to blindness after birth, likely employ physiological plasticity mechanisms (Knudsen, 1998; Mower et al., 1985; Röder et al., 2021), in order to re-adapt to the newly available visual excitation following sight restoration later in life.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the study's findings and cited literature

claim: Structural remodeling for typical E/I balance requires visual experience following birth.
source: Structural remodeling (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996) for typical E/I balance requires visual experience following birth (Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Takesian and Hensch, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018) and is linked to a sensitive period (Desai et al., 2002; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Structural remodeling for typical E/I balance is linked to a sensitive period.
source: Structural remodeling (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996) for typical E/I balance requires visual experience following birth (Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b; Takesian and Hensch, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018) and is linked to a sensitive period (Desai et al., 2002; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Desai et al., 2002; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005b

claim: A repeatedly documented finding in permanently congenitally blind humans is the increased thickness of visual cortex.
source: A repeatedly documented finding in permanently congenitally blind humans is the increased thickness of visual cortex (Anurova et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anurova et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2009

claim: Structural changes in permanently congenitally blind individuals were interpreted as a lack of experience-dependent pruning of exuberant synapses and/or reduced myelination.
source: These structural changes in permanently congenitally blind individuals were interpreted as a lack of experience-dependent pruning of exuberant synapses and/or reduced myelination, the latter typically leading to a shift of the grey-white matter boundary (Natu et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to Natu et al., 2019

claim: The overproduction of synapses during the initial phase of brain development was independent of experience in non-human primates.
source: In parallel, it was observed in non-human primates that the overproduction of synapses during the initial phase of brain development was independent of experience, but that synaptic pruning, predominantly of excitatory synapses, depended on visual experience (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996; Bourgeois et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996; Bourgeois et al., 1989

claim: Synaptic pruning, predominantly of excitatory synapses, depended on visual experience in non-human primates.
source: In parallel, it was observed in non-human primates that the overproduction of synapses during the initial phase of brain development was independent of experience, but that synaptic pruning, predominantly of excitatory synapses, depended on visual experience (Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996; Bourgeois et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bourgeois and Rakic, 1996; Bourgeois et al., 1989

claim: The lack of excitatory synapse pruning was thought to underlie the observed higher excitability of visual cortex due to congenital visual deprivation.
source: The lack of excitatory synapse pruning was thought to underlie the observed higher excitability of visual cortex due to congenital visual deprivation (Benevento et al., 1992; Huang et al., 2015; Morales et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benevento et al., 1992; Huang et al., 2015; Morales et al., 2002

claim: Increased visual cortex thickness has been observed for CC individuals following congenital blindness.
source: Crucially, increased visual cortex thickness (Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023) and higher BOLD activity during rest with the eyes open Rączy et al., 2022 have been observed for CC individuals following congenital blindness, suggesting incomplete recovery of cortical structure and function after sight restoration in humans.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023

claim: Higher BOLD activity during rest with the eyes open has been observed for CC individuals following congenital blindness.
source: Crucially, increased visual cortex thickness (Feng et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2015; Hölig et al., 2023) and higher BOLD activity during rest with the eyes open Rączy et al., 2022 have been observed for CC individuals following congenital blindness, suggesting incomplete recovery of cortical structure and function after sight restoration in humans.

claim: Increased visual cortex thickness and higher BOLD activity suggest incomplete recovery of cortical structure and function after sight restoration in humans.
